correctness.rationale: Four vertex projections give the two exact angular branches. Inverse-Jacobian transformation gives an explicit density with two monotonicity regimes. Square-root pole coefficients 2/pi, 4/pi, or 6/pi identify the long half-base and the existence of the interior extremum; support-minimum and right-density finite limit select the correct height phase. For the sole ambiguous phase, subtracting two known inverse-Jacobian branches leaves an indicator with support starting exactly at H, and the short half-base then follows from Q^2=(A+B)^2+H^2. A separate rectangle argument closes the boundary. All quantifiers A>B>0,H>0 (and A=B rectangles) are covered. Checkable script exercises thirteen strict/transition/rectangle configurations; its finite evidence is not substituted for the analytic proof.

originality.rationale: The inspected Akiyama–Kamae paper gives forward polygon-width representations and width-deviation optimization but not an inverse theorem from an unlabeled full law for all isosceles trapezoids. Martirosyan investigates orientation-dependent chord-length distributions/covariograms, not the unoriented marginal width law. Relevant published results address triangles, centrally symmetric tangential polygons or parallelograms; none of the inspected claims subsumes the proper isosceles-trapezoid inverse classification. The proof is a complete case analysis including coincident singularities rather than a parameter-renamed single prior example. Historical equivalence under other terminology remains possible.

value.rationale: This is a complete natural geometric inverse classification for an entire three-parameter non-centrally-symmetric quadrilateral family using only an unoriented one-dimensional projection-length law. It identifies a nontrivial finite singularity signature, treats multiple collisions and phase changes with one exact reconstruction method, and proves no two noncongruent isosceles trapezoids share the law. The precise recoverability question is meaningful in geometric tomography; it is not a mere evaluation of mean width, isolated computational example, or renamed result for centrally symmetric polygons.
